b1: 1269. A French army besieges *Lucera*, in Italy.
b2: One of its engineers, *Peter Peregrinus*, writes a letter about magnets.
b3: In it: a wheel that magnets would drive around *forever*.
c1: In the 1600s, English scholar *John Wilkins* describes a ramp.
c2: A magnet at the top pulls an *iron ball* up.
c3: It drops through a hole, rolls back down, and *climbs again*.
d2: says it will no longer deal with *perpetual motion*.
d3: Today, the U.S. patent office can demand a *working model*.
e1: So why does every magnet wheel *stop*?
e3: Every bit of help going in is *paid back* coming out.
e4: Over one full turn, the sum is *zero*.
e5: Friction takes the rest, and the wheel parks at its *sticky point*.
f2: Lodestone asks: what if the sticky point could be *switched off*?
g4: Trial two. A *shield* slides over the sticky point.
g5: 11 turns. Stopped. Moving the shield *costs what it saves*.
g6: Trial three. A *coil* fires at the sticky point and cancels the pull.
j1: Peregrinus wanted a wheel that *never stops*.
j2: We built one. It has a *plug*.
